subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Political Reform & the Suffrage Movement
subtitle: The extension of the vote from 1832 to 1928 and the campaign for women's suffrage.

data.targetWord: the right to vote in elections; when the franchise expands, more people are allowed to take part in choosing their representatives

examples.en-GB: The franchise expanded gradually from 1832 to 1928, moving from a few wealthy men to all adult men and women.

data.targetWord: a parliamentary constituency with very few voters that still elected MPs, often controlled by a wealthy landowner — criticised before the 1832 Reform Act

examples.en-GB: Old Sarum was a famous rotten borough with virtually no residents that still sent two MPs to Parliament before 1832.

data.targetWord: the law that removed many rotten boroughs, gave more seats to growing industrial towns, and extended the vote to more middle-class men, while still excluding most workers and all women

examples.en-GB: The 1832 Reform Act was an important step, but most working-class men and all women still could not vote after it passed.

data.targetWord: a working-class political movement of the 1830s and 1840s that campaigned for six democratic demands in the People's Charter, including votes for all men and secret ballots

examples.en-GB: Chartism grew because working-class men helped campaign for the 1832 Reform Act but gained no vote from it.

data.targetWord: the 1838 document setting out six Chartist demands: votes for all adult men, secret ballots, no property qualification for MPs, payment for MPs, equal electoral districts, and annual Parliaments

examples.en-GB: All but one of the People's Charter's six demands — annual Parliaments — eventually became part of British democracy.

data.targetWord: the law that made voting in elections private, so that voters could not be bribed or threatened because no one could see how they had voted

examples.en-GB: The Secret Ballot Act of 1872 made voting private, reducing bribery and intimidation at elections.

data.targetWord: the law that extended the vote to many urban working-class men, greatly increasing the electorate and making working-class voters important in towns and cities

examples.en-GB: The 1867 Reform Act was sometimes called the 'leap in the dark' because it gave the vote to many working-class men for the first time.

data.targetWord: the law that extended similar voting rights to many rural working-class men, making male voting rights more equal across town and countryside

examples.en-GB: The 1884 Reform Act meant that many agricultural labourers could vote for the first time, extending the franchise to rural Britain.

data.targetWord: a campaigner for women's votes who used peaceful, legal, and constitutional methods such as petitions, marches, speeches, and lobbying MPs

examples.en-GB: Millicent Fawcett led the suffragist campaign through the NUWSS, believing that peaceful methods would eventually persuade Parliament.

data.targetWord: a member of the Women's Social and Political Union who used more militant tactics to campaign for women's votes, including disrupting meetings, breaking windows, and hunger strikes

examples.en-GB: The slogan of the suffragettes was 'Deeds not words', reflecting their belief that peaceful methods had been ignored too long.

data.targetWord: the leader of the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, which used peaceful constitutional methods to campaign for women's voting rights

examples.en-GB: Millicent Fawcett led the NUWSS for decades, arguing that women deserved the vote because they obeyed laws and contributed to society.

data.targetWord: the founder of the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903, who led the militant suffragette campaign for women's votes

examples.en-GB: Emmeline Pankhurst's rallying cry 'Deeds not words' captured the WSPU's belief that direct action was necessary because peaceful methods had been ignored.

data.targetWord: the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, founded in 1897 and led by Millicent Fawcett, which used peaceful and constitutional methods to campaign for women's votes

examples.en-GB: The NUWSS grew into a large organisation with hundreds of local branches, campaigning peacefully for women's suffrage through meetings, petitions, and marches.

data.targetWord: the Women's Social and Political Union, founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst and others, which used militant methods including civil disobedience and property damage

examples.en-GB: The WSPU's militant campaigns made women's suffrage impossible to ignore, but also gave some opponents an argument against granting the vote.

data.targetWord: the law that gave the vote to all men over 21 and to some women over 30 who met property qualifications, after the First World War

examples.en-GB: The 1918 Representation of the People Act was important but unequal — women had to be over 30, while men could vote from 21.

data.targetWord: the law that gave women the right to vote on exactly the same terms as men, from age 21, completing equal political citizenship

examples.en-GB: The 1928 Equal Franchise Act finally gave women equal voting rights with men, completing nearly a century of campaigning.

data.targetWord: the violent breaking up of a peaceful reform meeting at St Peter's Field, Manchester, in 1819, when cavalry attacked the crowd, killing several people and injuring many

examples.en-GB: The Peterloo Massacre became a symbol of government repression and the need for parliamentary reform.

data.targetWord: a written request signed by many people, presented to an authority such as Parliament, asking for change — a key method used by Chartists and suffragists

examples.en-GB: Chartists presented massive petitions to Parliament in 1839, 1842, and 1848, gathering millions of signatures each time.

data.targetWord: a geographical area that elects a Member of Parliament; before 1832, constituencies were very unequal in size and representation

examples.en-GB: The Redistribution of Seats Act 1885 helped make constituencies more equal in size after decades of unfair representation.

data.targetWord: the popular name for the 1913 Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill Health) Act, which allowed hunger-striking suffragette prisoners to be released when ill and re-arrested when recovered

examples.en-GB: The Cat and Mouse Act was widely criticised because it seemed to use suffragettes' health as a tool to avoid the controversy of force-feeding.

data.targetWord: a system of government where people have a say in how they are ruled, usually through voting in free elections for representatives

examples.en-GB: Britain developed towards democracy gradually between 1832 and 1928 — it was not a sudden achievement but a long, contested process.

data.targetWord: a Chartist leader associated with 'moral force' Chartism, who believed in peaceful campaigning, political education, and constitutional methods

examples.en-GB: William Lovett represented the 'moral force' wing of Chartism, believing working people would earn the vote through demonstrating their education and respectability.

data.targetWord: a popular Chartist leader and newspaper owner who helped spread Chartist ideas through the Northern Star newspaper and mass meetings

examples.en-GB: Feargus O'Connor's Northern Star newspaper helped give Chartism a national audience and connected regional movements.

data.targetWord: a parliamentary constituency controlled by one powerful person or family, who could effectively choose which candidate became MP

examples.en-GB: In pocket boroughs, landowners could tell tenants how to vote, making real electoral competition virtually impossible.

data.targetWord: a form of protest in which a person refuses to eat, used by imprisoned suffragettes to draw attention to their cause and create political pressure on the government

examples.en-GB: Suffragette prisoners went on hunger strike to protest their treatment, forcing the government to choose between force-feeding or releasing them under the Cat and Mouse Act.

data.title: Put these reform milestones in chronological order
items: Peterloo Massacre at St Peter's Field, Manchester (1819)
First Reform Act — rotten boroughs removed, middle class gets vote (1832)
People's Charter published — six demands for democracy (1838)
Second Reform Act — many urban working men get vote (1867)
Third Reform Act — many rural working men get vote (1884)
Equal Franchise Act — women get equal voting rights from age 21 (1928)

data.title: Order these key events in the women's suffrage campaign
items: NUWSS formed under Millicent Fawcett — peaceful campaigning begins (1897)
WSPU founded by Emmeline Pankhurst — militant methods adopted (1903)
Suffragette window-smashing and arson campaigns intensify (1912-1913)
Cat and Mouse Act passed to deal with hunger-striking prisoners (1913)
Representation of the People Act — some women over 30 get vote (1918)
Equal Franchise Act — women and men vote on equal terms from 21 (1928)
